This study investigated the effects of cow’s milk on recovery from repeated simulated team games (STGs) in females. Twenty female team-sport athletes completed an STG circuit (2x ~ 30 min, with 10 min ‘half-time’). Measures of muscle function, soreness and tiredness, symptoms of stress and serum markers of muscle damage and oxidative stress were determined pre- and 24 h, 48 h, 72 h and 96 h following the circuit. At 48 h, a second STG was completed. Sprint performance (5 m, 15 m), lap time, countermovement jump (CMJ), heart rate and RPE were recorded during each STG. Immediately following each STG, participants consumed either 500 mL of cow’s milk (MILK) or 500 mL of an energy-matched carbohydrate (CHO) solution. Compared to CHO, MILK had a beneficial effect in attenuating losses in peak torque for knee extension (60°/s) (likely; effect size (ES) = 0.26 to 0.28) knee flexion (60°/s) (likely; ES = 0.45 to 0.61). A benefit for MILK was observed for 5 m sprint (possible-likely; ES = 0.40 to 0.58), 10 m sprint (likely; ES = 0.30 to 0.53) and symptoms of stress (likely–very likely, small). Mostly unclear outcomes for other variables were observed. For STG variables, trivial (HR, CMJ) and unclear (5 m sprint, 15 m sprint, lap-time, RPE) outcomes were recorded. In conclusion, the consumption of 500 mL of milk attenuated losses in muscle function and perceptions of stress following repeated simulated team-sports games. However, further investigation is warranted to determine whether MILK can influence subsequent team-sport performance. performance protein muscle damage post-exercise recovery female 1. Introduction Participation in a single team-sport match results in fatigue, muscle damage and oxidative stress in males [ 1 , 2 ] and females [ 3 , 4 ]. In reality, team-sport athletes engage in multiple training sessions or games within short periods of time resulting in insufficient recovery between bouts [ 5 , 6 , 7 ]. Recently, Mohr et al. [ 8 ] investigated responses to three soccer games played within one week, with male participants. Results indicated that the largest physiological stress, fatigue and decreased performance followed the second game which was preceded by only 3 days recovery. Based on this literature, opportunities exist to explore the responses of female team-sport athletes to repeated match play with short recovery duration. Minimizing muscle damage and enhancing recovery between training sessions or games could be beneficial for maintaining performance in subsequent bouts. Recent research has shown that the consumption of cow’s milk following muscle damaging exercise can attenuate decreases in muscle functional capacity in males [ 9 , 10 ] and females [ 11 , 12 ], perhaps due to an increase in post-exercise protein synthesis or a reduction in post-exercise degradation of muscle proteins [ 13 ]. It has also been reported that cow’s milk has anti-oxidant properties that may reduce oxidative stress [ 14 ] and the consumption of carbohydrate-protein mixtures may reduce lipid peroxidation [ 15 ]. The lack of effect of milk on exercise recovery reported in a number of investigations may be due to aspects of experimental design such as beverage blinding, homogeneity of participants, or the amount or timing of the cow’s milk intake [ 16 ]. To date, it is unknown whether the consumption of cow’s milk can enhance recovery from repeated match play, or whether a positive effect on recovery markers can influence subsequent match performance. Given the benefits of cow’s milk for enhanced recovery following muscle damaging protocols, and with the short recovery periods experienced by athletes between team-sport training sessions and games, it makes the expectation tenable that post-exercise consumption of cow’s milk may combat the negative effects of muscle damage and fatigue, thus accelerating the rate of recovery between matches. Accordingly, this study aims to examine the effect of cow’s milk on recovery from a simulated team game and a second simulated team game following a 48 h recovery period. Additionally, the effect of cow’s milk on ‘in-game’ measures in the second simulated game is explored.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Recovery from simulated team-sport match play, comparing milk (MILK) to carbohydrate (CHO) solution
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: MILK attenuated losses beneficially, showing likely to very likely benefits across 24h, 48h, and 72h post-exercise.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Small to moderate effect sizes (ES = 0.26-0.28 for extension; 0.45-0.61 for flexion). Quantified percentage differences indicated less decrement with MILK (e.g., extension at 24h: MILK -5.9% vs. CHO -10.0%).

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Recovery from simulated team-sport match play, comparing MILK to CHO. Also, within-game performance during STG2.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: MILK provided a beneficial effect, attenuating losses in performance across 24h-96h post-exercise. However, no benefit for absolute sprint performance was observed within STG2. A general decrease in 5m sprint performance was noted from STG1 to STG2 within-group, while 15m sprint performance showed a likely increase.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Small to moderate effect sizes (ES = 0.40-0.58 for 5m; 0.30-0.53 for 10m). Quantified percentage differences showed less decrement with MILK (e.g., 5m sprint at 24h: MILK -1.4% vs. CHO -3.1%).

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Recovery from simulated team-sport match play, comparing MILK to CHO solution.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: MILK attenuated increases in stress symptoms, showing a beneficial effect.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Small effect size, resulting in fewer 'worse than normal' symptoms over 24h, 48h, and 72h recovery.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Recovery following team-sport participation, comparing MILK to CHO solution.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Possible/likely beneficial effect for MILK, attenuating increases in soreness (at 24h) and tiredness (at 72h). Initially, both increased post-STG1.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Overall effect primarily unclear for both, but qualitative improvements noted (e.g., soreness at 24h: MILK 51.0% vs. CHO 65.5%).

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Post-exercise inflammatory response during recovery, comparing MILK to CHO solution.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Increased post-STG1. MILK consumption was associated with a harmful effect, showing increased levels compared to CHO at 2h, 24h, and 48h post-STG1. Post-STG2 outcomes were unclear for MILK vs. CHO.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Quantified differences showed higher hsCRP levels in the MILK group (e.g., B-2h: MILK 1.1x/÷1.6 vs. CHO 0.9x/÷1.6).

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Post-exercise oxidative stress response during recovery, comparing MILK to CHO solution.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Increased post-STG2 in MILK group. MILK consumption was associated with a harmful effect, showing increased levels compared to CHO at 24h post-STG1.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Quantified differences showed higher LOOH levels in the MILK group (e.g., B-24h: MILK 1.0x/÷1.2 vs. CHO 0.9x/÷1.2). Typically unclear for MILK vs CHO comparison overall.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Muscle function recovery, comparing MILK to CHO solution.
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Decreased post-STG1. Possible small harmful effect of milk on RSI at 72h and 96h post-exercise.
core_effect_and_quantification.magnitude_quantification: Quantified percentage differences indicated greater decrement with MILK (e.g., B-72h: MILK -17.3% vs. CHO -7.2%). Unclear overall.

core_effect_and_quantification.activity_context: Muscle damage marker post-exercise (STG1 and STG2).
core_effect_and_quantification.direction_of_change: Increased post-STG1 and post-STG2 (two-fold increase pattern). Unclear effect of cow's milk on accumulation.
Decreased post-STG1. Unclear outcomes for MILK vs CHO comparison and trivial outcomes during STG variables.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Post-strenuous simulated team-sport exercise and recovery, specifically investigating the impact of cow's milk consumption as a nutritional intervention in female athletes.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The beneficial effects of cow's milk on muscle function and recovery are speculatively linked to an enhancement of post-exercise protein balance, potentially by stimulating protein synthesis rates or reducing protein degradation. Additionally, cow's milk may possess anti-oxidant properties that contribute to reducing oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation, although explicit molecular mechanisms are not fully detailed within the observed biomarker changes.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study compared the immediate post-exercise consumption of 500 mL of cow's milk (MILK) (providing 17g protein or 0.26g/kg) against 500 mL of an energy-matched carbohydrate (CHO) solution following simulated team games (STG1 and STG2). While STG1 caused significant impairments in muscle function and increases in damage/inflammation markers, MILK generally showed benefits over CHO in attenuating losses in knee extension and flexion peak torque, 5m and 10m sprint performance, isokinetic soreness, tiredness, and symptoms of stress (DALDA B) at various post-exercise time points. However, MILK was associated with higher levels of hsCRP and LOOH in early recovery compared to CHO. No explicit dose-response for milk was investigated, and the 17g protein dose was noted as being below optimal thresholds for maximal protein synthesis.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Cow's milk demonstrated specific benefits over an energy-matched carbohydrate solution in attenuating losses in muscle function (peak torque for knee extension and flexion, 5m and 10m sprint performance) and reducing subjective symptoms such as stress, soreness, and tiredness following STG1. This positive effect was particularly evident during maximal performance scenarios. However, MILK showed a differential and potentially harmful effect on inflammatory (hsCRP) and oxidative stress (LOOH) markers in early recovery by increasing their levels compared to CHO. Furthermore, milk did not show benefit for absolute performance measures (sprint, jump height, lap times) within the second STG protocol, suggesting context-specific effects on recovery outcomes versus immediate subsequent performance.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Female team-sport athletes (N=20, age 20.6 +/- 3.0 years) engaged in amateur camogie and ladies Gaelic football, excluded for various health conditions or supplement use, undergoing strenuous simulated team-sport exercise.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Strenuous team-sport exercise leads to significant impairment in muscle function, increased muscle damage (CK), inflammation (hsCRP), and subjective reports of soreness and tiredness. Post-exercise consumption of cow's milk can offer a protective benefit by attenuating losses in muscle function (peak torque, sprint performance) and perceptions of stress, soreness, and tiredness, thereby enhancing recovery between training sessions or games and potentially aiding in maintaining subsequent performance. However, a notable implication is the potential adverse effect of milk on increasing inflammatory (hsCRP) and oxidative stress (LOOH) markers in the immediate post-exercise period. The persistent impairment of muscle function variables below baseline at 96 hours highlights challenges for athlete recovery in dense competition schedules.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Strenuous exercise itself presents an adverse risk due to muscle damage, inflammation, and performance impairment. The consumption of cow's milk provides a protective benefit for muscle function recovery and subjective perceptions of stress, soreness, and tiredness. However, there is a potential adverse risk associated with cow's milk consumption leading to higher levels of inflammatory (hsCRP) and oxidative stress (LOOH) markers in the early recovery phase. There is also a discussion of diagnostic utility regarding the validity of isolated sprint and jump performance metrics as indicators of overall recovery or predictors of actual match performance.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The assessment of biomarker reliability revealed mixed outcomes. While high-sensitivity procedures were used for CK and hsCRP, many variables showed 'unclear' or 'trivial' effects, particularly for oxidative stress markers post-STG1 and STG2 muscle function, indicating potential variability or insufficient statistical power. Specific measures like RFD and RSI exhibited considerable variability, possibly due to their technical demands. Subjective measures like soreness also had primarily unclear overall effects. The study noted that hsCRP might not fully reflect the overall cytokine response, and there were contradictory findings for oxidative stress markers (LOOHs, PCs) possibly due to differing analytical techniques or compartmentalization. A critical concern raised was the questioned validity and transferability of isolated sprint and jump performance as reliable markers of recovery or predictors of performance in real match situations, especially when athletes might not maximally perform during simulated games.
recommended_alternatives: Future investigations should critically assess the validity of recovery indicators, especially isolated sprint and jump performance, as predictors of actual match performance.
Future research should optimize protein intake levels, considering doses greater than 20g or even 40g for maximal stimulation of protein synthesis.
Further research is warranted to determine if hsCRP is truly reflective of the overall cytokine response.
Further investigation is needed to determine whether cow's milk can influence within-game performance variables when recovery periods are limited, focusing on different outcome contexts.
